author: claude
title: Whole-Cluster vs Destemmed Fermentation in Pinot

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: When red grapes arrive at the winery, they are still attached to their green stems. One of the first decisions a Pinot Noir maker faces is simple: keep the stems or remove them?

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Most wineries remove the stems with a machine. This is called destemming. The berries go into the tank alone. The result is often a wine with pure, clear fruit flavors, like fresh cherries and raspberries.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Other winemakers use whole clusters. This means putting complete bunches, stems and all, into the fermentation tank. Some use one hundred percent whole clusters, while others mix in only a portion. This is also called stem inclusion.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So what do the stems add? Many tasters notice spicy, herbal and floral aromas, such as tea, rose petals or white pepper. Some describe this as herbaceous lift, a fresh green note that makes the aroma feel more lively. The stems can also change the texture, adding fine tannins that feel silky rather than heavy.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: There is a risk, however. If the stems are not ripe, they can make the wine taste bitter and green. So whole clusters usually work best in good vintages, when stems have turned brown and woody.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Some of the most famous Burgundy producers are known for using a lot of whole clusters. Others never do. Neither approach is right or wrong. It is a question of style.
